summary: Defines the format of reputation response data (reputons), the media type to package it, and a registry for names of reputation applications and response sets. It is part of a small family of reputation documents.

eli5.summary: It decides what the answer card looks like when you ask whether something is trusted.

questions: what is the reputation applications registry
subtitle: A JSON answer card, the reputon, and the media type that carries ratings about names and things.

tldr.problem: Services that report how trustworthy something is (a domain, an address, anything with an identity) need a common shape for the answer so any client can read it.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7071 defines the reputon, a JSON object with a rater, an assertion, a rated subject and a rating from 0.0 to 1.0, plus the application/reputon+json media type and an IANA registry of reputation applications.
tldr.outcome: Any reputation query method can return the same data object. Each application registers its own assertions and extra keys, so clients can ignore what they do not understand.

facts.label: Rating precision
facts.value: SHOULD NOT exceed three decimal places

today: RFC 7071 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2013, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is meant to be used with the query method in RFC 7072.

sections.title: What the Document Defines
sections.content:
RFC 7071 defines a data object for answering a reputation query. It also defines a media type to carry that data when a transport follows the media type framework, such as the HTTP-based query method in RFC 7072. Future query methods are expected to reuse the same data object.

A third piece is an IANA registry holding definitions and symbolic names for known reputation applications and their response sets. The terms shared across the whole document series come from RFC 7070.
sections.eli5: It describes the shape of a reputation answer, gives that shape an official label, and starts a list where each kind of question gets its own entry.

sections.title: Reputon Attributes
sections.content:
A reputon is one independent object holding reputation information. A query about a subject gets back one or more of them. The format is JSON, and the media type is application/reputon+json, which takes no parameters. The body names the application context, and that name refers to a registration that defines the valid assertions and extensions for it.

Four attributes are common to every application:

  • rater: who computes and provides the information, typically a DNS domain name.
  • assertion: a keyword for the claim being rated.
  • rated: the identity of the entity being rated. Its form is application specific, and each application document must define its syntax and meaning.
  • rating: the overall score, a floating-point number from 0.0 to 1.0 inclusive.

Five more are OPTIONAL: confidence (certainty, also 0.0 to 1.0), normal-rating (what the provider would normally expect), sample-size (how many data points were used, an unsigned 64-bit integer), generated and expires (timestamps in seconds since January 1, 1970 00:00 UTC). A registered application may add its own attribute/value pairs.
sections.eli5: The report card says who gave the score, what it is about, who it is about and the score itself. It can also say how sure they are and how many people were asked.

sections.title: How Ratings Work
sections.content:
The rating is a number from 0.0 to 1.0. The RFC leaves it to each assertion's definition inside an application to declare what the anchor values 0.0 and 1.0 mean. Generally, 1.0 implies full agreement with the assertion and 0.0 indicates no support for it.

The definition also specifies the type of scale used when generating scores, and every reputation provider for that application must follow it.
sections.eli5: A score of 1.0 means "yes, totally" and 0.0 means "no support at all". What the score is about depends on the question being asked.

sections.title: Caching and Expiry
sections.content:
A reputon can carry an expires timestamp. After that time the client SHOULD NOT use the rating and SHOULD issue a new query. The RFC does not require clients to cache, though it sees obvious operational benefits. A stale cached rating can cause desirable traffic to be flagged as undesirable, or the reverse.

Reputation is typically most volatile when its subject is young. So if a service includes expiration timestamps, they SHOULD be lower for subjects about which little data has been collected.
sections.eli5: A score can go out of date, like milk. The expiry time tells you when to ask again, and new things should be rechecked sooner.

sections.title: The JSON Structure
sections.content:
A reputation object is a JSON object with two members: application (a string) and reputons (an array of reputons). Each reputon is an object whose members are the attributes above. Their order is not significant, and a given element MUST NOT appear more than once. rater, assertion, rated and rating are REQUIRED. Numeric ratings SHOULD NOT have more than three decimal places.

The set of keys used by one application is its response set. A client asking for the assertion sends-spam about example.com expects a reputon making that assertion and nothing more. If it names no assertion, the server can return reputons about any assertion it has data for, and the client ignores irrelevant ones.

An empty reputon is an acknowledgment that the request arrived and a positive indication that the server has no information. It is equivalent to a reputon with a sample-size of zero.
sections.eli5: The answer is a labelled box holding a list of report cards. An empty card means "I got your question but I know nothing about this".

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC's first example has the rater RatingsRUs.example.com consolidating 50000 data points and concluding that Alex Rodriguez scores 0.99 for the assertion is-good. As the RFC itself jokes, that does not say what he is good at.

A more specific baseball application can define assertions such as hits-for-power or strong-hitter, which make the same rating meaningful. A longer example uses the email-id application from RFC 7073: the rater rep.example.net reports that example.com appears associated with spam 1.2% of the time, based on 16938213 messages, with 95% confidence. It also uses an application-declared extension key, identity, to say how the subject was identified.
sections.eli5: A score of 0.99 for "is good" does not say what at. That is why each topic defines its own more precise questions.

sections.title: Media Type and Registry
sections.content:
IANA is asked to register the media type application/reputon+json (type application, subtype reputon+json, no required or optional parameters, "7bit" encoding sufficient, change controller IESG). Implementers may meet application values, attributes or response set items they do not support, and these are to be ignored.

IANA also creates the Reputation Applications registry. New entries follow the "IETF Review" or "Specification Required" policies. Each entry gives a symbolic name (a MIME token), a short description, the defining document and a status: current, deprecated or historic.

An application specification must be clear enough for interoperability: the subject of a query and its syntax, optionally a table of query parameters, a list of assertions with their 0.0 and 1.0 meanings and scale, and optional extension keys. Attribute names should be prefixed with the application name, so a foo application registers foo-bar, to avoid collisions.
sections.eli5: The official label is registered once. Then a public notebook lists each kind of reputation question, with the rules for answering it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it is primarily an IANA action registering a media type and does not describe a new protocol that might introduce security considerations. Security and operational impacts of reputation services in general are discussed in a separate work-in-progress document it cites.
sections.eli5: This RFC only defines the shape of the answer, so it says the safety questions belong to the documents about the services themselves.
